terms.meaning: Needs and wants are unlimited, but the resources to meet them are limited. So we must choose.
terms.example: There is not enough land in a city for every use people want.

terms.meaning: Because of scarcity, people, firms and governments must decide how to use limited resources.
The value of the next best thing you give up when you make a choice.
terms.example: If you spend Saturday working, the opportunity cost might be a day skiing.

terms.meaning: A good with no opportunity cost, because using it takes nothing away from anyone else.
terms.example: Air to breathe.

terms.meaning: The resources used to make goods and services: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
Natural resources used in production, such as soil, water, forests and minerals.
The physical and mental effort people put into producing goods and services.
Man-made goods used to produce other goods, such as machines, tools and buildings.
Organising the other factors of production and taking risks to start or run a business.
A diagram showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all its resources used fully and efficiently, with given technology.
Some resources, such as workers or machines, are not being used. The economy produces at a point inside its PPC.
Using all resources fully, with no waste. On a PPC, every point on the curve is efficient.
An increase in output from using unemployed resources. On a PPC it is a movement from a point inside the curve towards the curve.
An increase in what the economy is able to produce, from more or better resources or technology. The PPC shifts outward.
Each extra unit of one good costs more and more of the other good, because resources are not equally good at making both. The PPC bows outward.
Each extra unit of one good always costs the same amount of the other good. The PPC is a straight line.
Latin for “all other things being equal”. We change one thing at a time and assume everything else stays the same.
Statements about what is, was or will be. They can be tested with evidence.
terms.example: “A higher bus fare reduced the number of riders.”

terms.meaning: Statements about what ought to be. They are based on value judgments and cannot be tested.
terms.example: “Bus fares should be free.”

terms.meaning: The quantities of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices in a given time period, ceteris paribus.
As the price of a good falls, the quantity demanded rises, ceteris paribus. Price and quantity demanded are inversely related.
The amount consumers are willing and able to buy at one particular price.
A change in quantity demanded or supplied caused only by a change in the good’s own price.
The whole curve moves because a non-price determinant changed. More or less is demanded or supplied at every price.
Things other than the good’s own price that shift demand: income, tastes and preferences, future price expectations, prices of related goods, and the number of consumers.
A good whose demand rises when income rises. Its YED is positive.
A good whose demand falls when income rises, because people switch to better alternatives. Its YED is negative.
terms.example: Instant noodles for some consumers.

terms.meaning: Goods that can be used in place of each other. If the price of one rises, demand for the other rises.
terms.example: Tea and coffee.

terms.meaning: Goods used together. If the price of one rises, demand for the other falls.
terms.example: Skis and lift tickets.

terms.meaning: When price falls, a consumer’s real income (buying power) rises, so they can buy more.
When a good’s price falls, it becomes cheaper compared with other goods, so consumers switch towards it.
As a person consumes more units of a good, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit falls.
The quantities of a good that producers are willing and able to sell at different prices in a given time period, ceteris paribus.
As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus.
The amount producers are willing and able to sell at one particular price.

Things other than the good’s own price that shift supply: costs of factors of production, prices of related goods (joint and competitive supply), indirect taxes and subsidies, future price expectations, technology, and the number of firms.
Two goods produced together from the same process, so more of one means more of the other.
terms.example: Beef and leather.

terms.meaning: Two goods that compete for the same resources, so making more of one means making less of the other.
terms.example: A farmer choosing between wheat and canola.

terms.meaning: A tax on spending on goods and services, paid to the government by the seller. It raises firms’ costs, so supply shifts left (up).
A payment from the government to producers for each unit. It lowers firms’ costs, so supply shifts right (down).
The price and quantity where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. There is no pressure for the price to change.
At a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied.
At a price above equilibrium, quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded.
The way prices change to allocate resources in a market, through signalling, incentive and rationing.
A change in price sends information to buyers and sellers about where resources are wanted.
A change in price motivates buyers and sellers to change what they do, for example producing more when the price rises.
A higher price limits who buys a scarce good to those willing and able to pay it.
The difference between the highest price consumers are willing to pay and the price they do pay. It is the area below the demand curve and above the price.
The difference between the price producers receive and the lowest price they would accept. It is the area above the supply curve and below the price.
Consumer surplus plus producer surplus. It is greatest at the competitive market equilibrium.
Resources are used to make the goods society values most. It happens where marginal benefit equals marginal cost (MB = MC), and community surplus is maximized.
The extra benefit from consuming one more unit. The demand curve shows marginal benefit.
The extra cost of producing one more unit. The supply curve shows marginal cost.
Community surplus that is lost because the market is not at the allocatively efficient quantity.
How much quantity demanded responds to a change in price. PED = %change in quantity demanded ÷ %change in price.
PED is greater than 1 (ignoring the minus sign). Quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price.
PED is between 0 and 1 (ignoring the minus sign). Quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than price.
PED equals 1. Quantity demanded changes by the same percentage as price, so total revenue does not change.
PED is infinite. The demand curve is horizontal.
PED is zero. Quantity demanded does not change when price changes. The demand curve is vertical.
The money a firm receives from sales: price × quantity sold (P × Q).
(new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100.
A way to remember what makes PED high or low: Habits, Income share, Necessity, Time, Substitutes.
Number and closeness of substitutes, degree of necessity, proportion of income spent on the good, and time. Many classes also add habits (HINTS).
How much demand responds to a change in income. YED = %change in quantity demanded ÷ %change in income.
Raw materials from farming, fishing, forestry and mining, such as coffee beans, wheat or copper.
How much quantity supplied responds to a change in price. PES = %change in quantity supplied ÷ %change in price.
A legal highest price, set by the government below the equilibrium price. Also called a price ceiling. It causes a shortage.
terms.example: A limit on rents so that tenants pay less.

terms.meaning: A legal lowest price, set by the government above the equilibrium price. Also called a price floor. It causes a surplus.
terms.example: A minimum price for wheat, or a minimum wage.

terms.meaning: A minimum price for labour: the lowest wage firms may legally pay per hour. If it is above the equilibrium wage, it can cause a surplus of labour (unemployment).
terms.example: A law that shop workers must earn at least $20 an hour.

terms.meaning: People or groups affected by a decision or policy, such as consumers, producers, workers and the government.
terms.example: A sugar tax affects drink buyers, drink makers and the government budget.

terms.meaning: How the burden of an indirect tax is shared between consumers and producers. The side with the less elastic curve pays more of the tax.
terms.example: Demand for cigarettes is price inelastic, so smokers pay most of a cigarette tax.

terms.meaning: Meeting the needs of people today without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
terms.example: Catching fish no faster than they can breed keeps the fish stock sustainable.

terms.meaning: Every society must decide what and how much to produce, how to produce it, and for whom.
terms.example: Should a village build houses or boats (what), with machines or by hand (how), and who gets them (for whom)?

terms.meaning: An economic system where private owners and prices answer the basic economic questions, with very little government intervention.
terms.example: Firms make whatever buyers are willing and able to pay for.

terms.meaning: An economic system where the government owns most resources and decides what, how and for whom to produce.
terms.example: A planning office sets how many shoes each factory must make.

terms.meaning: An economic system that uses both markets and government intervention to answer the basic economic questions. Almost all real economies are mixed.
terms.example: Shops are private, but schools and hospitals are paid for by taxes.

terms.meaning: A model of the economy. Money flows from firms to households as incomes, and back to firms as spending. Goods, services and factors of production flow the other way.
terms.example: You earn wages from a shop, then spend them at a café. The café pays its workers, and the money keeps flowing.

terms.meaning: Money that leaves the circular flow of income: savings, taxes and spending on imports.
terms.example: A family puts part of its pay in the bank. That money does not go straight back to firms as spending.

terms.meaning: Money that enters the circular flow of income from outside the household and firm loop: investment, government spending and exports.
terms.example: A firm borrows to build a new factory. That investment adds spending to the economy.

terms.meaning: An opinion about what is good, right or fair. It cannot be proved or disproved with evidence.
terms.example: "Taxes on the rich should rise" contains a value judgement: "should".

terms.meaning: A possible explanation or prediction that can be tested with evidence.
terms.example: Hypothesis: when bus fares fall, more people take the bus.

terms.meaning: Information from observing or measuring the real world, used to test a theory.
terms.example: Counting bus trips before and after a fare cut.

terms.meaning: Showing with evidence that a theory is wrong. A refuted theory is replaced or changed.
terms.example: If bus trips do not rise after a fare cut, the hypothesis is refuted.

terms.meaning: Fairness. What is fair is a value judgement, so people disagree about it.
terms.example: Some people think a fair tax system takes a bigger share from people with higher incomes.

terms.meaning: Everyone having the same, for example the same income or the same opportunities.
terms.example: Equal pay for the same job is an example of equality.

terms.meaning: The idea that markets work best with very little government intervention. Linked to Adam Smith in the 18th century.
terms.example: Letting prices, not the government, decide what firms produce.

terms.meaning: A cost or benefit that falls on third parties, people outside the market who did not choose it.
terms.example: Smoke from a factory makes people nearby cough.

terms.meaning: The free market does not allocate resources efficiently, so it makes too much or too little of a good. Externalities are one cause.
The quantity where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost (MSB = MSC). Society is best off here: allocative efficiency.
The extra benefit to the buyer from one more unit. It is the demand curve.
The extra cost to the producer of one more unit. It is the supply curve.
The extra benefit to society from one more unit: the buyer's benefit plus any external benefit, or minus any external cost, of consumption.
The extra cost to society of one more unit: the firm's cost plus any external cost, or minus any external benefit, of production.
A good that is good for people and society, but is underconsumed in a free market, often because of a positive consumption externality.
terms.example: Education and vaccines.

terms.meaning: A good that harms the user and others, and is overconsumed in a free market.
terms.example: Cigarettes.

terms.meaning: A tax on each unit of a good with a negative externality. It should equal the external cost at the social optimum, so the market makes Q*.
A tax on the carbon content of fuels, so firms and households pay for the harm from carbon emissions.
The government caps total pollution and issues permits for it. Firms can buy and sell the permits, so firms that can cut pollution cheaply do so.
Laws and rules that limit or ban an activity, with fines for breaking them.
terms.example: A noise law that limits loud music at night.

terms.meaning: Government education campaigns that give people better information, so demand moves towards MSB.
terms.example: Health warnings about smoking.

terms.meaning: The government makes or runs a good itself, often free or cheap, to raise its consumption.
terms.example: Free public schools and vaccines.

terms.meaning: PES is greater than 1. Quantity supplied changes by a bigger percentage than price.
terms.example: A T-shirt factory with idle machines can raise output by 30% when the price rises 10%.

terms.meaning: PES is between 0 and 1. Quantity supplied changes by a smaller percentage than price.
terms.example: A coffee farm raises output by only 5% when the price rises 25%, because new trees take years to grow.

terms.meaning: PES equals 1. Quantity supplied changes by the same percentage as price. Any straight supply curve from the origin has PES = 1.
A period so short that firms cannot change their output at all. Supply is perfectly inelastic (PES = 0).
terms.example: The fish already on the boat are all that can be sold this morning.

terms.meaning: A period in which at least one factor of production, such as land or machines, is fixed. Firms can add workers and materials.
terms.example: A car factory adds a night shift on the same assembly lines.

terms.meaning: A period long enough for all factors of production to change, and for new firms to join the market.
terms.example: A car maker builds a second factory.

terms.meaning: Machines, buildings or workers that a firm is not using fully. With unused capacity a firm can raise output quickly, so supply is more elastic.
terms.example: A factory where half the machines stand idle.

terms.meaning: How easily a producer can keep goods to sell later. Goods that can be stored have more elastic supply, because stock can be sold as soon as the price rises.
terms.example: Canned soup keeps for a long time; fresh flowers wilt in days.

terms.meaning: How easily land, labour and capital can move into a new use. More mobile factors make supply more elastic.
terms.example: Any rider with a bike can start working for a delivery service, but a shipyard needs specialist welders.

terms.meaning: Goods made in factories from raw materials, such as phones, bicycles or chocolate bars.
A diagram showing how quantity demanded of a good changes as income changes. Income is on the vertical axis and quantity demanded is on the horizontal axis.
terms.example: A flat section shows a luxury, a steep section a necessity, and a section that bends back an inferior good.

terms.meaning: A normal good with a YED above 1: quantity demanded rises by a bigger % than income. Many services are luxuries.
terms.example: Restaurant meals and holidays abroad.

terms.meaning: A normal good with a YED between 0 and 1: quantity demanded rises by a smaller % than income.
terms.example: Bread and milk.

terms.meaning: A firm's ability to set its own price instead of accepting the market price. The fewer close substitutes and the higher the barriers to entry, the more market power.
A market with many small firms selling the same (homogeneous) product, with free entry and exit. Each firm is a price taker and has no market power.
terms.example: Many farmers growing the same kind of wheat.

terms.meaning: A market with many firms and free entry, where each firm's product is a bit different. Each firm has a little market power.
terms.example: A street of cafés, hair salons or restaurants.

terms.meaning: A market with a few large firms and high barriers to entry. The firms are interdependent: each one must think about how its rivals will react.
terms.example: Airlines, mobile networks, supermarket chains.

terms.meaning: A market with a single or dominant firm, high barriers to entry and no close substitutes. The firm is a price maker.
A market where economies of scale are so large that one firm can supply the whole market at a lower average cost than two or more firms could.
terms.example: Water pipes or an electricity grid.

terms.meaning: Anything that makes it hard for new firms to enter a market, such as high set-up costs, economies of scale, patents, licences or strong brands.
A firm that must accept the market price, because it is too small to change it. Firms in perfect competition are price takers.
A firm with market power that can choose its price. It faces a downward sloping demand curve, so a higher price means fewer sales.
Making a product a bit different from rivals' products, for example by quality, style, brand or location.
In an oligopoly, each firm's best choice depends on what its rivals do, so firms must think about how rivals will react.
The total market share of the largest firms in a market. CR4 is the combined share (%) of the four largest firms. A high ratio means a few firms dominate.
terms.example: Shares of 30%, 25%, 15% and 10% give CR4 = 80%.

terms.meaning: The extra revenue from selling one more unit: the change in total revenue. For a firm with market power, MR is below the price.
Revenue per unit sold: TR ÷ Q. Average revenue equals the price, so the demand curve is the AR curve.
Cost per unit: total cost ÷ quantity (TC ÷ Q).
Profit above normal profit. It happens when AR > AC, so TR is greater than TC.
The profit a firm needs to stay in business. It happens when AR = AC, so TR = TC. Economists count normal profit as part of costs.
When firms work together instead of competing, for example by agreeing to keep prices high. Formal collusion (a cartel) is illegal in many countries.
A formal agreement between firms to fix prices or limit output, so they act like one monopoly. Cartels are illegal in many countries.
A game in which each player's dominant strategy leads to an outcome that is worse for both than if they had cooperated.
terms.example: Two cafés both cut prices and both earn less than if both kept prices high.

terms.meaning: Competing in ways other than price, such as advertising, loyalty schemes, quality or new products. Common in oligopoly, where price cuts are quickly copied.
Falls in average cost as a firm grows and produces more.
terms.example: A big water company spreads the cost of its pipes over millions of homes.

terms.meaning: Money the government pays to people without asking for a good, service or factor in return. They give an income to people the market pays little or nothing.
terms.example: Unemployment benefits, disability benefits and pensions.

terms.meaning: One side of a deal knows more than the other, for example about the quality of a good or about its own behaviour. It can cause market failure.
terms.example: The seller of a used car knows about its faults. The buyer does not.

terms.meaning: Hidden information about quality or risk before a deal. The side that knows less pays an average price, so the best products or lowest-risk buyers leave the market.
terms.example: Owners of good used cars will not sell at the average price, so mostly lemons are left.

terms.meaning: One side changes its behaviour after a deal and takes more risk, because the other side carries the cost and cannot see what it does.
terms.example: A driver takes more risks once insured. A bank takes big risks because it expects a bail-out.

terms.meaning: A used good of poor quality whose faults the buyer cannot see before buying.
A private response to asymmetric information: the side that knows more shows its quality in a way that is costly to fake.
terms.example: A seller offers a warranty. A job applicant shows a degree.

terms.meaning: A private response to asymmetric information: the side that knows less takes steps to find the hidden information.
terms.example: A buyer pays for a car inspection. An insurer asks for a health check.

terms.meaning: A government response to asymmetric information: the government gives people the facts, often for free.
terms.example: Public safety ratings for car models, or hygiene scores for restaurants.

terms.meaning: Resources that are rivalrous but non-excludable: one person's use leaves less for others, but it is hard to stop people from using them.
terms.example: Fish in the open ocean, forests and groundwater.

terms.meaning: When people acting in their own self-interest overuse a shared resource, so it runs down and everyone loses.
terms.example: Every boat catches as many fish as it can, and the fish stock collapses.

terms.meaning: A good is rivalrous when one person's use leaves less for others.
terms.example: A fish you catch cannot be caught by anyone else.

terms.meaning: A good is non-excludable when it is hard or impossible to stop people from using it, even if they do not pay.
terms.example: No one can keep boats out of the open ocean.

terms.meaning: A limit on the quantity of something that can be produced, caught or traded.
terms.example: Each boat may land only 2 tonnes of cod a week.

terms.meaning: The users of a shared resource make, monitor and enforce their own rules for using it.
terms.example: Villagers who share a lake agree catch limits, take turns checking, and fine anyone who cheats.

terms.meaning: Agreements between countries to act together on a shared problem, such as fish stocks or pollution that cross borders.
terms.example: Countries that share a sea agree limits on the total catch.

terms.meaning: A good that is non-rivalrous and non-excludable. The free market may provide too little of it, or none at all.
terms.example: Streetlights, national defence and a lighthouse.

terms.meaning: A good is rivalrous when one person's use leaves less for others. It is non-rivalrous when one more user takes nothing away from anyone else.
terms.example: A pizza is rivalrous. A streetlight is non-rivalrous: one more person walking under it does not dim the light.

terms.meaning: A good is excludable when people who do not pay can be stopped from using it. It is non-excludable when nobody can be kept out.
terms.example: A cinema is excludable. A fireworks display in the sky is non-excludable.

terms.meaning: People enjoy a good without paying for it, because they cannot be stopped from using it. If many people free ride, nobody will pay to provide the good.
terms.example: A neighbour pays nothing towards the streetlights but still walks home in their light.

terms.meaning: A good that is rivalrous and excludable. The free market can provide it, because sellers can charge everyone who uses it.
terms.example: A pizza or a T-shirt.

terms.meaning: A good that is excludable but non-rivalrous (until it gets crowded). Not named in the IB guide, but useful for sorting goods.
terms.example: A gym membership or a toll road.

terms.meaning: The government makes or runs a good itself, with its own workers, and pays for it with taxes.
terms.example: A national army, or council workers who run the streetlights.

aliases: contracting out to the private sector
terms.meaning: The government pays a private firm to make or run a good. Taxes still pay for it, and the government decides what is provided.
terms.example: A council pays a private firm to fit and run its streetlights.

terms.meaning: The standard model of how consumers choose. It assumes they are rational, maximize utility and have perfect information.
The assumption that consumers think carefully and choose the option that is best for them.
The assumption that consumers choose to get the most satisfaction (utility) they can from their income.
The assumption that consumers know everything about every choice, such as prices and quality.
A branch of economics that uses ideas from psychology to study how people really make choices.
A mental shortcut or habit of thinking that leads to choices that are not fully rational.
A simple mental shortcut used to make a choice quickly, instead of comparing every option.
terms.example: Always buying the brand you bought last time.

terms.meaning: A bias: people rely too much on the first number or fact they see, and judge later choices against it.
terms.example: A "was $200" tag makes a $120 price look cheap.

terms.meaning: A bias: the same facts, described in a different way, change the choice people make.
terms.example: "90% fat free" sounds healthier than "10% fat".

terms.meaning: A bias: things that are easy to bring to mind, such as vivid news, seem more common or likely than they are.
terms.example: Fearing sharks after reading shark stories.

terms.meaning: People have limited time, information and brain power, so they settle for a choice that is good enough.
People plan well but give in to what they want now, against their own long-term interest.
terms.example: Planning to save, then spending the money on a treat.

terms.meaning: People care about others and about fairness, not only about their own gain.
terms.example: Giving to charity or leaving a tip.

terms.meaning: Buyers or sellers do not have all the facts they need to make the best choice.
The way choices are designed and set out for people. It can change what people choose.
An option that is chosen for people in advance. They keep it unless they opt out.
terms.example: Workers are put into a pension plan unless they leave it.

terms.meaning: The number of options is limited, to make choosing easier or to remove harmful options.
terms.example: A canteen menu with a short list of healthy meals.

terms.meaning: People must make a choice for themselves. Nothing is chosen for them in advance.
terms.example: Answering yes or no to organ donation on a licence form.

terms.meaning: Small changes to how choices are presented can push people towards better choices, without banning options or changing incentives much.
terms.example: Putting fruit at eye level in a canteen.

terms.meaning: A business objective: earn the largest possible profit, total revenue minus total cost.
A business objective: act ethically towards workers, communities and the environment, even if it costs more.
A firm's sales as a share of all sales in the market. Some firms aim to make it bigger.
A business objective: aim for a satisfactory level of profit, enough to keep stakeholders happy, not the most possible.
A business objective: get bigger, with more sales revenue, output, sites or workers.
